answers.answer:
The distribution of NAD(P)-binding in SCOPe 2.08 points to repeated, independent recruitment of dinucleotide-binding modules into different structural contexts, so it is mainly evidence of convergent evolution of a ligand-binding function. It is not by itself evidence of divergent descent from one ancestor.

What the classification shows: c.2.1 (NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains, sunid 51735) sits in fold c.2. c.3.1 (FAD/NAD(P)-binding domain, sunid 51905) sits in a different fold, c.3. d.81.1 (GAPDH-like C-terminal domain, sunid 55347) sits in fold d.81 and is a different class (a+b). The Rossmann-type c.2 fold and the FAD/NAD(P) c.3 fold are topologically distinct, so SCOP does not place them in one fold, and SCOP's fold level is defined to allow independent origins. Within one superfamily (for example c.2.1) SCOP treats members as probably homologous. Across folds, no common ancestry is asserted.

Divergent versus convergent: sharing a superfamily (e.g. c.2.1 members) supports divergent evolution from a common ancestor. Sharing only a binding function across folds (c.2 vs c.3 vs d.81) is best read as convergence, or as a binding solution found more than once. The GAPDH case shows the point well: from pretrained knowledge, the NAD-binding region of GAPDH is an N-terminal Rossmann-type domain (c.2.1), while the C-terminal catalytic domain is d.81.1. The cofactor site and the catalytic domain therefore come from different folds within one enzyme. Multidomain enzymes can have a binding module that is homologous to one family while the rest of the protein has a different origin.

Why cofactor binding or active-site similarity is not sufficient for homology: (1) A dinucleotide pocket requires a few physicochemical features (a loop with a glycine-rich motif such as GxGxxG, a helix N-terminus for the pyrophosphate, and adenine-ribose contacts). Many unrelated folds can supply these, so the function is reachable from many starting structures. (2) Short motifs recur by chance or by convergence and are often shared by proteins that are not dehydrogenases, so a motif match gives false positives. (3) Shared chemistry or a shared cofactor says what the protein binds, not where it came from. Homology needs evidence of common ancestry: consistent core topology and strand order over most of the structure, sequence or profile relationships beyond the motif, and agreement across independent structural comparisons. (4) Function transfer is a separate step. Same cofactor does not imply same reaction, substrate, or regulation. Oxidoreductase families differ in substrate specificity and catalytic residues even when the cofactor is shared.

Limits and caveats: the SCOPe classification and tool results here establish superfamily and fold membership and their parent lineage. They do not by themselves establish homology between two specific proteins, exact domain boundaries, or the NAD-binding role of any particular sequence. The GAPDH domain-to-fold assignment is from pretrained knowledge. A search for 'NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domain' in release 2.08 returned no hits, so that search did not add evidence. Any claim about a specific enzyme should be checked against that enzyme's own SCOPe domain record and against structure-based and sequence-based comparisons. Representative selection can also bias which folds appear.
